sub_topic: What is Statistics, Data and Data types
title: What is Statistics
content:
Statistics is a scientific method that concerns data collection, presentation, analysis, interpretation or inference about data when issues of uncertainties are involved.

Statistics is broadly classified into:
(i) Descriptive statistics — data collection, summarizing and comparing numerical data. Concerned with summarizing a data set rather than using the data to learn about the population.
(ii) Inferential statistics — techniques and tools for collecting data from a population by studying a sample, gaining knowledge of the population characteristics and making vital decisions about the sampled population.

Statistics is useful in Accountancy, Engineering, Education, Business, Social Sciences, Law, Agriculture and any human area of endeavour where decision making is of vital importance.

sub_topic: Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary Sources
title: Sources of Data
content:
Primary data are information collected by a researcher specifically for the research at hand — original, current and directly related to the issue. Collected by the researcher himself through methods like interviews, surveys, questionnaires.

Secondary data are obtained from already existing records or sources — derived from published or unpublished records of government agencies, trade associations, research bureaus, magazines and individual research work.

Scrutiny of secondary data checks Reliability, Suitability and Adequacy.

Internal source: data collected within the organization (sales receipts, invoice, work schedule).
External source: data collected outside the organization.

title: Descriptive vs Inferential Statistics
content:
Descriptive statistics deals with data collection, summarizing and comparing numerical data. Concerned with summarizing a data set rather than using the data to learn about the population.

Inferential statistics deals with techniques and tools for collecting data from a population by taking a sample. Knowledge of population characteristics is gained and decisions are made about the sampled population.

title: Population, Sample, Statistics and Parameter
content:
Population: the entire group of individuals or items about which we want information or draw conclusions.

Sample: a part of the population observed for the purpose of making scientific statements about the population.

Parameter: a numerical characteristic of a population (e.g. population mean μ, population standard deviation σ).

Statistic: a numerical characteristic computed from a sample (e.g. sample mean x̄, sample standard deviation s).

title: Quantitative and Qualitative Data
content:
Quantitative data: numerical values.
- Discrete: integer values (e.g. number of books sold, number of registered students).
- Continuous: real numbers — integer, fraction or decimal (e.g. heights, weights, prices).

Qualitative data: no numerical values; cannot be represented by numbers.
- Ordinal Non-numeric: ranking is allowed (e.g. beauty contest judgement).
- Nominal Non-numeric: classification by group or category (e.g. level of education, sex, occupation).

title: Variable
content:
A variable is a characteristic that can take on different values. Variables can be classified as:

- Quantitative variable: numerical values (discrete or continuous).
- Qualitative variable: categories or attributes (nominal or ordinal).

Variables can also be classified by role:
- Independent variable (X): the explanatory or predictor variable.
- Dependent variable (Y): the response or outcome variable.

title: Hypothesis
content:
A hypothesis is an assumption or guess about the population parameters involved. Used to aid decision making.

There are two types:
- Null hypothesis (H₀): states that there is no difference between the procedures, samples and other phenomenon.
- Alternative hypothesis (H₁): any hypothesis which differs from the null hypothesis.

Example: if population mean μ = 5.0 and sample mean x̄ = 6.0:
H₀: μ = x̄  (i.e. 5.0 = 6.0)
H₁: μ ≠ x̄  or  μ < x̄  or  μ > x̄

title: Steps in Hypothesis Testing
content:
The procedure for carrying out a significance test about a population parameter:

(a) Set up the hypothesis about the parameter of interest and state its significance level.
(b) Set the hypothesis by using the appropriate test statistic.
(c) Draw conclusion by making decision on the result of your computed value in step (b). The table value at the given significance level is compared with the computed value.

title: One-tailed and Two-tailed Tests
content:
The type of test depends on the stated alternative hypothesis (H₁).

One-tailed (one-sided) test: alternative hypothesis is one directional.
Examples: H₁: μ > x̄ or H₁: μ < x̄

Two-tailed (two-sided) test: hypothesis is of two directions.
Example: H₁: μ ≠ x̄

The significance level used depends on the test:
- For one-tailed at significance level α, check critical value at α.
- For two-tailed at significance level α, check critical value at α/2.

sub_topic: Type I and Type II Errors
title: Type I and Type II Errors
content:
Type I error: rejecting a hypothesis which is supposed to be accepted.
Type II error: accepting a hypothesis which is supposed to be rejected.

Decision table:

| Decision | H₀ true | H₀ false |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accept H₀ | Correct decision | Type I error |
| Reject H₀ | Type II error | Correct decision |

The level of significance (α) is the maximum probability of being willing to risk a Type I error. Common values: 1% (0.01) and 5% (0.05). The investigator has (1 − α) confidence of making a right decision.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 1 (T-test) including differences between two population means
title: T-test (Small Sample)
content:
For small samples (n < 30), the test statistic is the t-test, assuming the sampling distribution is approximately normal.

Test statistic for population mean:
t = (x̄ − μ₀) / (s / √n)

where s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)

For difference between two population means (independent samples):
t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / √[s²(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)]    (with pooled variance s²)

Decision: compare t-calculated with t-table at (n − 1) degrees of freedom at the given significance level. If |t-cal| > t-table, reject H₀; otherwise accept H₀.

The t-distribution table is at /tables/t.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient
title: Chi-square Test of Independence
content:
A statistic used to test the hypothesis that the row and column variables are independent.

H₀: The two variables are independent.
H₁: The two variables are dependent.

Test statistic:
χ² = Σ (Oᵢ − Eᵢ)² / Eᵢ

where Oᵢ is the observed frequency and Eᵢ is the expected frequency in cell i.

Degrees of freedom: (r − 1)(c − 1), where r is the number of rows and c is the number of columns in the contingency table.

Decision: reject H₀ if χ²-calculated > χ²-table at the given significance level.

Requirements:
1. Sample must be randomly drawn.
2. Data must be raw frequencies (not percentages).
3. Variables are assumed independent.
4. Categories must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
5. Expected values should not be less than 5 (rule of five); collapse categories otherwise.

The chi-square table is at /tables/chisquare.

title: Bivariate Regression Analysis
content:
Bivariate data involve two variables. Regression analysis examines the relationship between them.

The simple linear regression model of y on x:
y = a + bx

where:
- y = dependent (response) variable
- x = independent (explanatory) variable
- a = intercept on the y-axis (the point where the line cuts the y-axis)
- b = regression coefficient — the slope or gradient of the line

Methods of fitting:
(i) Graphical method: draw a scatter diagram, fit a straight line by inspection.
(ii) Algebraic method: use the least squares normal equations.

Note: It is important to distinguish the independent and dependent variables, which is not necessary for correlation.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis
content:
When Y depends on more than one X (say X₁, X₂), the multiple regression model is:

Y = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + ε

The normal equations (from least squares, summing the residual to zero) are:
ΣY = nb₀ + b₁ΣX₁ + b₂ΣX₂
ΣX₁Y = b₀ΣX₁ + b₁ΣX₁² + b₂ΣX₁X₂
ΣX₂Y = b₀ΣX₂ + b₁ΣX₁X₂ + b₂ΣX₂²

Solve the three simultaneous equations for b₀, b₁, b₂ using Cramer's rule (determinant method) or matrix inversion.

Testing utility of the model:
H₀: β₁ = β₂ = ... = βₖ = 0
H₁: at least one βᵢ ≠ 0

title: Inferences Concerning the Regression Slope
content:
Estimates of the regression coefficients a and b (least squares):

b = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) / (nΣx² − (Σx)²)

a = ȳ − bx̄

Application and interpretation of b:
1. b is the slope of the regression line.
   - If b > 0: upward sloping — y increases as x increases.
   - If b < 0: downward sloping — y decreases as x increases.
2. The regression line can be used for prediction: given x, compute ŷ = a + bx.

Test for significance of b uses the t-test with (n − 2) degrees of freedom.

title: Interpretation of Regression Coefficients
content:
In y = a + bx:
- a (intercept): the predicted value of y when x = 0. May have no practical meaning if x = 0 is outside the data range.
- b (regression coefficient): the amount by which y changes for a one-unit change in x. Holds other variables constant in multiple regression.

For multiple regression Y = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂, each bᵢ is interpreted holding the other independent variables constant.

Goodness of fit:
- Coefficient of determination r²: proportion of variation in y explained by x. r² closer to 1 means better fit.

title: Product Moment Correlation Coefficient (Pearson)
content:
Karl Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient measures the degree of linear relationship between two variables x and y. The value of r lies between −1 and +1 (−1 < r < 1).

r = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) / √[(nΣx² − (Σx)²)(nΣy² − (Σy)²)]

Alternative forms:
r = covariance(x, y) / √[var(x) · var(y)]

Interpretation:
- r close to +1: perfect positive linear relationship.
- r close to −1: perfect negative linear relationship.
- r close to 0: no linear relationship.

Example: r = +0.92 → good correlation; r = −0.12 → poor correlation.

title: Spearman Rank Correlation
content:
Used when values are in ranks (ordinal scale) rather than actual measurements — e.g. beauty contest ranking.

R = 1 − [6Σdᵢ² / (n(n² − 1))]

where dᵢ is the difference in each pair of ranks and n is the number of objects ranked.

R = +1 when ranks are in perfect agreement; R = −1 in perfect disagreement; otherwise −1 < R < 1.

Tie handling: when ties occur, each tied value is given the mean of those ranks (e.g. if two places are tied for second, each takes (2+3)/2 = 2.5).

Spearman is easier to compute than Pearson but is generally less accurate.

title: Inferences Concerning Correlation Coefficient
content:
To test the significance of a correlation coefficient r:

H₀: ρ = 0  (population correlation is zero)
H₁: ρ ≠ 0

Test statistic (for n > 30):
t = r√(n − 2) / √(1 − r²)

Compare |t| with t-table at (n − 2) degrees of freedom.

For small n, use a table of critical r values directly.

A significant r means the observed correlation is unlikely to be due to chance alone.

title: Interpretation of Correlation Coefficient
content:
Three types of simple correlation by value:

1. Positive correlation: as one variable increases, the other also increases. Example: income and expenditure.

2. Negative correlation: as one variable increases, the other decreases. Example: number of labourers and time required to complete work.

3. Zero correlation: no relationship between the variables.

Strength:
- |r| close to 1: strong linear relationship.
- |r| close to 0: weak or no linear relationship.

Note: correlation does not imply causation — a strong r does not prove that x causes y.

title: Test of Linearity
content:
The product moment correlation coefficient r measures the strength of a linear relationship only. A scatter diagram is the first check for linearity.

If the scatter diagram suggests a non-linear (curvilinear) relationship, Pearson's r may underestimate the true association. In such cases, consider:
- Transforming variables (e.g. log x, √x) and recomputing r.
- Using a non-linear correlation measure.

Empirical rule: if |r| > 0.7 and the scatter is roughly linear, the linear model is a reasonable description.

title: Index Number
content:
An index number is a statistical measure designed to show changes in a variable (or group of variables) over time or across geographical locations.

Spiegel: 'A statistical measure designed to show changes in a variable or group of variables over time or for geographical locations.'

Uses of index numbers:
- Measure changes in prices, quantities or values over time.
- Compare activity across regions.
- Track inflation and cost of living.
- Forecast future economic activity.

title: Price and Quantity Relative Indices
content:
Price Relative Index (PRI):
PRI = (Pₙ / P₀) × 100

where Pₙ is the price in the current year and P₀ is the price in the base year.

Quantity Relative Index (QRI):
QRI = (qₙ / q₀) × 100

where q� is the quantity in the current year and q₀ in the base year.

title: Value Index
content:
The value index (or value relative index) measures changes in total monetary worth. It combines price and quantity changes.

VRI = (pₙqₙ / p₀q₀) × 100 = (Vₙ / V₀) × 100

where Vₙ = p� × qₙ and V₀ = p₀ × q₀.

title: Simple and Weighted Aggregate Indices
content:
Simple Aggregate Price Index (SAPI):
SAPI = (Σpₙ / Σp₀) × 100

Simple Aggregate Quantity Index (SAQI):
SAQI = (Σqₙ / Σq₀) × 100

Simple Average of Price Relatives:
SAPRI = (Σ(pₙ/p₀ × 100)) / N

Weighted indices (below) give different commodities appropriate weights rather than treating them equally.

title: Laspeyre's Index
content:
Laspeyre's price index uses base year quantities as weights.

LAPI = (Σpₙq₀ / Σp₀q₀) × 100

Laspeyre's quantity index uses base year prices as weights.

LAQI = (Σqₙp₀ / Σq₀p₀) × 100

title: Paasche's Index
content:
Paasche's price index uses current year quantities as weights.

PAPI = (Σpₙqₙ / Σp₀qₙ) × 100

Paasche's quantity index uses current year prices as weights.

PAQI = (Σqₙpₙ / Σq₀pₙ) × 100

title: Fisher's Ideal Index
content:
Fisher's Ideal Index combines base year and current year quantities/prices as weights. It is the geometric mean of Laspeyre's and Paasche's indices.

FIPI = √[(Σpₙq₀ / Σp₀q₀) × (Σpₙqₙ / Σp₀qₙ)] × 100

title: Marshall-Edgeworth Index
content:
Marshall-Edgeworth's index uses an average of the base-year and current-year quantities as weights.

MEI = [(Σpₙq₀ + Σpₙq�) / (Σp₀q₀ + Σp₀qₙ)] × 100

A related form is the Dorbish-Booley index, which takes the simple arithmetic mean of Laspeyre's and Paasche's price indices:

DBI = [(Σpₙq₀ / Σp₀q₀ + Σpₙqₙ / Σp₀qₙ) / 2] × 100

title: Problems in Construction of Index Numbers
content:
Likely problems:
- Selection of base year — sometimes arbitrary or biased.
- Selection of items to be compared.
- The choice of an appropriate average.
- The choice of an appropriate weight.
- What is the appropriate formula to use?

title: Uses of Index Numbers
content:
Index numbers are used to:
- Measure changes in the general price level over time.
- Measure changes in quantity (volume) traded.
- Compare economic activity across regions.
- Track inflation and the cost of living.
- Inform policy decisions (wages, pensions, taxes).
- Forecast future trends in prices and quantities.

title: Time Series
content:
A time series is a sequence of data points measured at successive points in time. Time series analysis is used for forecasting future values — e.g. given 25 years of price data, predict the price for year 26.

Two model forms:

Additive model:
Xₜ = Tₜ + Sₜ + Cₜ + I�

Multiplicative model:
Xₜ = Tₜ × Sₜ × C� × Iₜ

title: Components of a Time Series
content:
Four components:

1. Trend or Secular Trend (Tₜ): the long-term movement of the series — continuous growth, stagnation or decline.

2. Seasonal Variation (Sₜ): the identical or almost identical patterns a time series appears to follow during corresponding periods of successive years (e.g. cloth prices during festive periods, umbrella/woollen prices in winter vs summer).

3. Cyclical Variation (C�): long-term oscillations or swings about a trend line — wave-like movement, may or may not be periodic. Example: movement of sales and income in prosperity and depression.

4. Irregular Variation (Iₜ): the random, sporadic component due to chance or unpredictable events (fire, flood, strike, earthquake).

title: Models of Time Series
content:
Two classical models:

Additive model:
Xₜ = Tₜ + Sₜ + Cₜ + Iₜ

The components are assumed independent and of similar magnitude. Useful when seasonal variation is roughly constant over time.

Multiplicative model:
Xₜ = Tₜ × S� × Cₜ × Iₜ

Components interact. The seasonal variation is proportional to the trend. Most common in practice.

sub_topic: Estimation of Trends: Moving Average Method
title: Moving Average Method
content:
A k-yearly moving average at time t is the arithmetic mean of k consecutive values centred at t.

Example: for Y values 20, 35, 43, 49, 52, 57 (years 2006–2011):
3-yearly moving averages:
(20+35+43)/3 = 32.67 (at 2007)
(35+43+49)/3 = 42.33 (at 2008)
(43+49+52)/3 = 48.00 (at 2009)
(49+52+57)/3 = 52.67 (at 2010)

Advantages:
1. Easy to compute.
2. Eliminates periodic/seasonal movements.

Limitations:
1. Loss of information at extreme ends.
2. Not a good means of comparing trends.

sub_topic: Estimation of Trends: Method of Least Squares
title: Method of Least Squares for Trend
content:
Fit a straight line trend ŷ = a + bt where t is the time index (years).

Normal equations (same as regression):
Σy = na + bΣt
Σty = aΣt + bΣt²

Solving:
b = (nΣty − ΣtΣy) / (nΣt² − (Σt)²)
a = ȳ − bx̄ₜ

To reduce arithmetic, shift the origin so Σt = 0 (e.g. for odd n, centre t at 0; for even n, centre between two middle periods).

sub_topic: Estimation of Trends: Deviation Method of Trend Estimation
title: Deviation Method
content:
An alternative to least squares using deviations from a chosen origin.

If A is the assumed mean and dᵢ = yᵢ − A, then:

trend values = A + (Σdᵢ / n)

For trend lines, you can also fit:
ŷ = A + b · t
where t is the deviation of the time variable from the chosen origin.

title: Seasonal Variation (Simple Methods)
content:
Simple methods to estimate seasonal variation:

1. Simple average method: for each season, compute the average of its values over all years. Express each seasonal average as a percentage of the overall (grand) average — this gives the seasonal index.

2. Ratio-to-trend method: divide each actual value by the corresponding trend value (from the fitted line) to get a percentage. Average the percentages for the same season across years.

3. Ratio-to-moving-average method: divide each actual value by the centred moving average. The averages of these ratios for each season give the seasonal index.

The seasonal indices for a complete cycle should sum to 400 (quarterly), 1200 (monthly) or 100 × k for k periods.
